2.3 1.3 Data Cleaning & Variable Engineering


Code
# Create analysis-ready dataset
dat_raw <- pcod |>
  select(year, X, Y, depth, density, present) |>
  filter(!is.na(density))

# Engineer variables
dat <- dat_raw |>
  mutate(
    # Response transformations
    log_density = log(density + 0.01),

    # Temporal variables
    fyear = as.factor(year),
    year_scaled = scale(year)[,1],

    # Depth variables (multiple transformations for model flexibility)
    depth_c = scale(depth)[,1],          # Centered & scaled
    depth_c2 = depth_c^2,                # Quadratic
    log_depth = log(depth + 1),          # Log-transformed
    sqrt_depth = sqrt(depth),            # Square root

    # Spatial variables
    X_c = scale(X)[,1],
    Y_c = scale(Y)[,1],

    # Regional indicator (North/South split)
    region = factor(ifelse(Y > median(Y), "North", "South")),

    # Interaction term
    region_year = interaction(region, fyear)
  )

3.1.1 2.1.1 Nominal Abundance Trend

# Calculate nominal index
nominal_index <- dat |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_density = mean(density),
    se = sd(density) / sqrt(n()),
    median_density = median(density),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(nominal_index, aes(x = year, y = mean_density)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean_density - 1.96*se,
                  ymax = mean_density + 1.96*se),
              alpha = 0.2, fill = "blue") +
  labs(title = "Nominal Abundance Index (Unstandardized)",
       subtitle = "Simple mean density per year",
       x = "Year", y = "Mean Density (kg/km²)") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2003, 2017, 2))

text:
6.1 5.1 Standardization Strategy
Goal: Create a prediction grid where covariates are held at reference values except year.
Reference values:
For GLMM (parametric depth): - Depth → mean depth (centered = 0) - Region → modal category
For GAM (spatial smooth): - Depth → sequence covering range (for marginal effects) - X, Y → grid covering survey area (for spatial integration)

title: Comprehensive Abundance Index Standardization Workflow with standard methods
text:
6.2 5.2 Prediction Grid for GLMM


Code
# Calculate reference values
ref_depth <- mean(dat$depth)
ref_depth_c <- (ref_depth - mean(dat$depth)) / sd(dat$depth)
ref_depth_c2 <- ref_depth_c^2
ref_region <- names(sort(table(dat$region), decreasing = TRUE))[1]

# Build prediction grid WITH ALL VARIABLES USED IN MODEL
pred_glmm <- expand.grid(
  year = sort(unique(dat$year)),
  depth_c = ref_depth_c,
  depth_c2 = ref_depth_c2,
  log_depth = log(ref_depth + 1), 
  region = ref_region,
  X = mean(dat$X),  
  Y = mean(dat$Y)
) |>
  mutate(
    fyear = factor(year, levels = levels(dat$fyear))
  )

# Now predict
pred_link_glmm <- predict(best_glmm, newdata = pred_glmm,
                          type = "link", se.fit = TRUE,re.form = NA)

title: Day 1: Foundations
text:
Day 1: Monday, May 4
Theme: Foundations of Abundance Indices and Spatial Autocorrelation

08:30 - 10:00 | Session 1: Foundations of Abundance Indices

08:30 - 08:50 | Welcome & Introductions (20 min)

Ice-breaker, participant background review, and workshop logistics.

08:50 - 09:15 | Module 1: From Raw Observations to Biological Signals (25 min)

Why standardize? Isolating true abundance from noise (vessel effects, gear changes, environment).

09:15 - 10:00 | Module 2: The Evolution of Standardization Models (45 min)

The journey from GLM to GAM: handling non-linearities, random effects, and Delta-models.




10:00 - 10:15 | Morning Break ☕


10:15 - 12:00 | Session 2: Hands-on Lab 1 – Classic Frameworks

Building a robust time series from fisheries data.
Practice with mgcv and lme4 using survey and fisheries-dependent datasets.
Key task: Diagnosing fit with DHARMa and extracting standardized indices.



12:00 - 13:15 | Lunch Break 🍴


13:15 - 14:45 | Session 3: Mapping the Latent Ocean – The Spatial Engine

The Core Issue: Independence vs. Autocorrelation. Why Tobler’s Law matters for fisheries.
The Gaussian Random Field (GRF): Modeling the “invisible sheet” of spatial density.
The SPDE Approach: Solving complex spatial math using a triangulated Mesh to create continuous surfaces.



14:45 - 15:00 | Afternoon Break ☕


15:00 - 16:00 | Session 4: Hands-on Lab 2 – Spatial Scaffolding

Building the Scaffolding: Creating and testing your first Mesh in sdmTMB.
Playing with Space: Modeling spatial autocorrelation and visualizing mesh residuals.
Demo: Identifying spatial bias and “ghost” patterns in the residuals.

title: Day 2: S-T Fusion
text:
Theme: Spatio-Temporal Fusion – Adding the Fourth Dimension

08:30 - 10:00 | Session 5: Dynamics in Space and Time

Module 5: Beyond static maps—how abundance surfaces evolve.

Understanding the temporal component of fish density.

Core Concepts:

Autoregressive structures (AR1): Modelling dependencies between years.
Random Walks: Handling non-stationary trends in time.
Spatio-temporal correlations: How space and time interact.




10:15 - 12:00 | Session 6: Hands-on Lab 3 – Conceptualising our first S-T Model

Fitting spatio-temporal GLMMs using sdmTMB.
Visualizing “The Movie”: Generating and comparing annual abundance surfaces to see shifts in distribution.

title: The Magic Map
text:
Outline

The challenge — discrete dots in a fluid ocean
Foundational principle — Tobler’s First Law
The Gaussian Random Field (GRF)
The Matérn covariance function
The “Big N” problem
The SPDE approach — meshes & sparsity
Integrating the field into the model
The resulting Magic Map



Pre-requisite: Module 3 — Generalized Linear Models for ecological count data.

title: The Magic Map
section: Discrete dots in a fluid ocean
text:
Discrete dots in a fluid ocean


The input
Data at discrete sampling locations:
\[
s_i = (\text{Longitude}, \text{Latitude})_i
\]
Each tow, station, or transect is one point in space.

The illusion
Standard regression treats each \(s_i\) as independent — as if every point were surrounded by a vacuum.








Biological truth


Fish populations form a continuum. A 500 kg catch at point \(A\) implies similar density 500 m away. Independence is a modelling fiction we must repair.

title: The Magic Map
text:
Tobler’s First Law

“Everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things.”
— Waldo Tobler, 1970


Like weather: if it rains at your house, it is probably raining at your neighbour’s. Fish density behaves the same way.








Why we cannot ignore it


Spatial autocorrelation clumps the error term \(\varepsilon\). The consequences:

biased fixed-effect estimates (covariates absorb spatial structure they did not cause)
overconfident standard errors → too-narrow confidence intervals
inflated Type-I error in hypothesis tests

title: The Magic Map
text:
The invisible sheet
A Gaussian Random Field (GRF) is a stochastic process where any finite collection of points follows a multivariate normal distribution:
\[
\boldsymbol{\omega} = \big(\omega(s_1), \ldots, \omega(s_n)\big) \sim \mathcal{N}_n(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})
\]

Imagine an elastic sheet draped over the study area:


Peaks
High density pushes the sheet upward.

Valleys
Low density lets it sink.

Smooth slopes
Stretchiness ensures continuity between neighbours.

title: The Magic Map
section: The Matérn covariance — rules of the sheet
text:
The Matérn covariance — rules of the sheet
The texture and stiffness of the GRF. For two points at distance \(d_{ij} = \lVert s_i - s_j \rVert\):
\[
\operatorname{Cov}\!\big(s_i, s_j\big) \;=\; \sigma^{2}\,\frac{1}{2^{\nu-1}\Gamma(\nu)}\,(\kappa\, d_{ij})^{\nu}\,K_{\nu}(\kappa\, d_{ij})
\]


Range — \(r\)
Distance beyond which spatial correlation effectively vanishes.
\[r = \sqrt{8\nu}\,/\,\kappa\]

Marginal SD — \(\sigma\)
Magnitude of spatial variability — the wave height of the sheet.




\(K_\nu(\cdot)\) is the modified Bessel function of the second kind; \(\nu\) controls smoothness (commonly fixed at \(\nu = 1\) in 2-D SPDE work).

title: The Magic Map
text:
The “Big N” problem
A continuous GRF requires inverting a dense \(n \times n\) covariance matrix.



Step
Cost




Build \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\)
\(\mathcal{O}(n^{2})\) memory


Invert / Cholesky \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\)
\(\mathcal{O}(n^{3})\) time


Likelihood evaluation per iteration
\(\mathcal{O}(n^{3})\)




With \(n \approx 5{,}000\) tows, this breaks any laptop — and surveys routinely hit \(10{,}000\)+ records.



We need a representation of the GRF that is continuous in space but sparse in computation.

title: The Magic Map
section: The SPDE approach — the spider web
text:
The SPDE approach — the spider web
Lindgren, Rue & Lindström (2011) showed that a Matérn GRF is the stationary solution of a stochastic partial differential equation:
\[
(\kappa^{2} - \Delta)^{\alpha/2}\,\big(\tau\,\omega(s)\big) = \mathcal{W}(s)
\]

Solve it on a triangulated mesh — a finite set of knots:


Knots
Field values are computed only at triangle vertices.

Barycentric interpolation
Within each triangle, values are linearly blended.

Result
Sparse precision matrices replace dense covariance — fast and scalable.

title: The Magic Map
section: Designing the mesh — precision vs. performance
text:
Designing the mesh — precision vs. performance


Inner zone

high triangle density
in the data-rich region
high precision, slower

Outer buffer zone

larger triangles
prevents edge leakage and numerical instability
cheap to compute


R Lab — build your mesh
library(sdmTMB)

mesh <- make_mesh(
  data    = catch_df,
  xy_cols = c("X", "Y"),
  cutoff  = 15            # km between knots
)

plot(mesh)
The cutoff argument controls knot spacing — smaller values yield finer meshes.









Tip


Rule of thumb: target the cutoff at roughly 1/5 of your expected spatial range \(r\).

title: The Magic Map
section: Integrating the field into the model
text:
Integrating the field into the model
The spatially explicit linear predictor adds the GRF term \(\omega(s_i)\) to the fixed effects:
\[
\log(\mu_i) \;=\; \underbrace{\beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{Depth}_i + \beta_2\,\text{Temp}_i}_{\text{fixed effects}} \;+\; \underbrace{\omega(s_i)}_{\text{latent spatial field}}
\]



Fixed effects
Measured covariates — depth, temperature, sediment.

\(\omega(s_i)\)
Absorbs unmeasured drivers: hidden currents, habitat structure, social behaviour.

INLA / sdmTMB
Fast (approximate) Bayesian inference in R — no MCMC required.

title: The Magic Map
text:
A reproducible fit in sdmTMB
library(sdmTMB)

fit <- sdmTMB(
  formula = catch_kg ~ depth_s + temp_s,
  data    = catch_df,
  mesh    = mesh,
  family  = tweedie(link = "log"),
  spatial = "on"
)

tidy(fit, effects = "ran_pars", conf.int = TRUE)
#> term        estimate  conf.low  conf.high
#> range       42.6      31.2      58.1
#> phi          1.18      1.05      1.32
#> sigma_O      0.91      0.74      1.12


Equivalent INLA workflow: inla.spde2.pcmatern() → inla.stack() → inla().

title: The Magic Map
text:
The resulting Magic Map


What you gain

Corrected uncertainty — confidence intervals reflect true spatial patchiness; no more overconfident predictions.
Prediction anywhere — estimate density at any \((\text{Lon}, \text{Lat})\), including unsampled locations.
Honest covariate effects — fixed effects are no longer contaminated by spatial structure.
Diagnostic value — the shape of \(\hat{\omega}(s)\) reveals the missing covariate you have not yet measured.


Predict on a new grid
grid <- expand.grid(
  X = seq(xmin, xmax, by = 2),
  Y = seq(ymin, ymax, by = 2)
)

preds <- predict(
  fit,
  newdata     = grid,
  return_tmb_object = TRUE
)

# Posterior mean + SE per cell
head(preds$data[, c("est", "est_se")])

title: The Magic Map
text:
Make the map dynamic
The field \(\omega(s)\) we just fit is frozen in time.
But fish move. Habitats shift. Climate drifts.

How does the spatial field evolve across years?
